note: Typical mistakes are tendencies, not rules about people. They happen because your first language has different sounds, letters or rules – this is called transfer (or interference). Not everyone makes these mistakes, and many learners stop making them quite quickly. If you know where a mistake comes from, you get rid of it faster. Based on contrastive linguistics (comparing language systems, e.g. Swan & Smith, Learner English, Cambridge University Press) and experience from English language teaching.

languages.name: English
strengths: English and Spanish share thousands of words from Latin: hospital, animal, importante, familia.
English has the th of “think”, so the /θ/ of Spain (gracias, cerveza) isn't new to you.

mistakes.wrong: pero, perro with an English r (tongue curled back)
mistakes.right: pero: one tap · perro: several taps
mistakes.why: English r doesn't touch the top of the mouth. Spanish r does: one quick tap for r, a little like the tt in American “butter”, and several for rr.

mistakes.wrong: “noh-oo”, “teh-LEH-fuh-noh” (no, teléfono)
mistakes.right: no, teléfono: every vowel short and clear
mistakes.why: In English, weak syllables turn into a short “uh” (/ə/), and many vowels glide. Spanish vowels keep their full sound in every syllable.

mistakes.wrong: “p-hapá”, “t-homate”, “k-hasa” (with a puff of air)
mistakes.right: papá, tomate, casa: no puff
mistakes.why: At the start of a word, English p, t, k come with a puff of air. Spanish p, t, k have none, so the puff sounds foreign straight away.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with top teeth on the bottom lip
mistakes.right: vino, nuevo: only the lips
mistakes.why: English has a separate v sound. Spanish doesn't: b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: “cara” for cada, “toro” for todo (a quick tap)
mistakes.right: cada, todo: soft d, like th in “this”
mistakes.why: Between vowels, English d is often a quick tap, and to Spanish ears that is an r. Spanish d there is soft, like th in “this”.

mistakes.wrong: zapato, plaza with a buzzing z
mistakes.right: zapato, plaza: /θ/ as in “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: English z buzzes, but Spanish has no such sound. In most of Spain z is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south it is s. Both are correct; the buzz isn't.

mistakes.wrong: hola, hotel, hospital with a breath at the start
mistakes.right: “ola”, “otel”, “ospital”
mistakes.why: English h is a breath. Spanish h is silent.

languages.name: German
strengths: Many words are related: house – Haus, water – Wasser, book – Buch.
Same alphabet, and a simple sentence often has the same order: I drink coffee – Ich trinke Kaffee.

mistakes.wrong: “tsapato”, “tsine” (zapato, cine)
mistakes.right: zapato, cine: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: German z is ts, and so is c in words like Celsius. Spanish has no ts here: in most of Spain it is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south s.

mistakes.wrong: “fino”, “Falencia”, “wino” (vino, Valencia)
mistakes.right: vino, Valencia: only the lips
mistakes.why: German v is f or v, and w is v. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only: vino starts like Bein.

mistakes.wrong: sopa, museo with a buzzing s
mistakes.right: sopa, museo: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: German s before a vowel often buzzes (Sonne, Rose). Spanish s doesn't: it is the sharp s of das.

mistakes.wrong: pero, perro with an r in the throat
mistakes.right: pero: one tap · perro: several taps
mistakes.why: Most German r sounds are made in the throat, or disappear at the end of a word (Vater). Spanish r is made with the tongue tip, and you always hear it.

mistakes.wrong: “p-hapá”, “t-homate”, “k-hasa” (with a puff of air)
mistakes.right: papá, tomate, casa: no puff
mistakes.why: German p, t, k come with a puff of air. Spanish p, t, k have none.

mistakes.wrong: mi |amigo, en |España (a small stop before the vowel)
mistakes.right: “mia-mi-go”, “e-nes-pa-ña”
mistakes.why: German starts a word on a vowel with a small stop in the throat (Knacklaut). Spanish lets words run together.

mistakes.wrong: “Madrit”, “ciudat”, “ustet”
mistakes.right: Madrid, ciudad, usted: a very soft d
mistakes.why: In German, d at the end of a word becomes t (Hund). In Spanish it stays very soft, close to th in English “this”.

mistakes.wrong: hola, hora with a breath at the start
mistakes.right: “ola”, “ora”
mistakes.why: German h at the start of a word is a breath. Spanish h is silent.

mistakes.wrong: Can I become a coffee, please?
mistakes.right: Can I have a coffee, please?
mistakes.why: False friend: bekommen = get or have. become = werden. More of them: also = so, Chef = boss, Handy = mobile, aktuell = current.

mistakes.wrong: I live here since three years.
mistakes.right: I've lived here for three years.
mistakes.why: German uses the present + seit. English uses the present perfect, with for + a length of time (since + a point in time: since 2022).

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I have worked until six.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I worked until six.
mistakes.why: German uses the Perfekt for most things in the past. With a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2019), English uses the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: The informations are on the website.
mistakes.right: The information is on the website.
mistakes.why: German Informationen is a plural. In English, information is uncountable: no -s, and the verb is singular (is).

mistakes.wrong: In the Summer I speak english with my Friends.
mistakes.right: In the summer I speak English with my friends.
mistakes.why: German writes every noun with a capital, but nationality words with a small letter (englisch). English does the opposite: nouns small, languages, nationalities, days and months capital.

languages.name: French
strengths: Many English words come from French: table, restaurant, information, government.
French and English have the same basic order: Je bois du café – I drink coffee.

mistakes.wrong: pero, perro with a French r in the throat
mistakes.right: pero: one tap · perro: several taps
mistakes.why: French r is made in the throat. Spanish r is made with the tip of the tongue, behind the top teeth.

mistakes.wrong: pan, bien, tiempo with a French nasal vowel
mistakes.right: “pa-n”, “bie-n”, “tiem-po”: clean vowel + n
mistakes.why: In French, n or m after a vowel often makes the vowel nasal and is not said itself. Spanish vowels stay clean, and you say the n or m.

mistakes.wrong: tú, luna, música with the French u of “tu”
mistakes.right: tú, luna, música: u like French “ou”
mistakes.why: French has two sounds here. Spanish u is always the “ou” of vous.

mistakes.wrong: stress at the end: “telefonó”, “medicó”
mistakes.right: teléfono, médico: stress on the accent
mistakes.why: French stresses the end of a word or phrase. Spanish stress can fall on different syllables, and moving it can change the word: hablo, habló.

mistakes.wrong: jamón, gente with the soft j of “je”
mistakes.right: jamón, gente: a rasp at the back of the mouth
mistakes.why: French j and ge are soft. Spanish j and ge are a rasp, close to the French r.

mistakes.wrong: casa, mesa with a buzzing s
mistakes.right: casa, mesa: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: In French, s between vowels buzzes (maison, rose). Spanish s doesn't.

mistakes.wrong: “musho”, “shico” (mucho, chico)
mistakes.right: mucho, chico: ch as in “tchèque”
mistakes.why: French ch is sh. Spanish ch starts with the tongue touching the roof of the mouth, like tch in “tchèque”.

mistakes.wrong: I have 25 years.
mistakes.why: French says j'ai 25 ans (I have). English says: I'm 25, or I'm 25 years old.

mistakes.wrong: I am here since two weeks.
mistakes.right: I've been here for two weeks.
mistakes.why: French uses the present + depuis. English uses the present perfect + for (a length of time) or since (a point in time).

languages.name: Portuguese
strengths: Portuguese and Spanish share most of their everyday words: casa, mesa, família, trabalho – trabajo.
Portuguese nh (banho) is the same sound as Spanish ñ (baño).

mistakes.wrong: “pocu”, “nochi”, “mes'” (poco, noche, mesa)
mistakes.right: poco, noche, mesa: clear o, e, a
mistakes.why: Portuguese weakens vowels that aren't stressed: final o and e become u and i in Brazil, and nearly vanish in Portugal. Spanish vowels stay clear.

mistakes.wrong: jamón, gente with the soft Portuguese j
mistakes.right: jamón, gente: a rasp at the back of the mouth
mistakes.why: Portuguese j and ge are soft, as in “gente”. Spanish j and ge are a rasp, like ch in Scottish “loch”.

mistakes.wrong: “cahro”, “hojo” (carro, rojo)
mistakes.right: carro, rojo: taps of the tongue tip
mistakes.why: Portuguese r at the start of a word and rr are often made in the throat, or sound like h in much of Brazil. Spanish rr and first r are several taps of the tongue tip.

mistakes.wrong: casa, mesa with a buzzing s; “dosh” for dos
mistakes.right: casa, mesa, dos: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: In Portuguese, s between vowels buzzes, and in Portugal and Rio a final s sounds like sh. Spanish s is the sharp s of “sol”.

mistakes.wrong: bien, son like “bem”, “são”
mistakes.right: “bie-n”, “so-n”: clean vowel + n
mistakes.why: Portuguese makes vowels nasal before n and m, and in ã and õ. Spanish vowels stay clean, and you say the n or m.

mistakes.wrong: “shico”, “musho” (chico, mucho)
mistakes.right: chico, mucho: ch as in “tchau”
mistakes.why: Portuguese ch is sh (chave). Spanish ch is the sound of tch in “tchau”.

mistakes.wrong: “cale”, “polo” (calle, pollo)
mistakes.right: calle, pollo: y as in “yes”
mistakes.why: Portuguese doesn't write ll, so it looks like a plain l. In most of Spain it sounds like y.

languages.name: Italian
strengths: Many English words come from Latin, like Italian ones: important, possible, family, university.
Italian has the sounds of ch in chair and j in jam (ciao, giorno).

mistakes.wrong: “chena”, “tsapato” (cena, zapato)
mistakes.right: cena, zapato: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: In Italian, c before e, i is the sound of “cena”, and z is ts or dz. In Spanish, in most of Spain, both are /θ/; in Latin America and much of the south, s.

mistakes.wrong: “jente” (gente) with the Italian g of “gelato”
mistakes.right: gente, trabajo: a rasp at the back of the mouth
mistakes.why: Italian g before e, i is soft. Spanish g before e, i, and j, are a rasp, like ch in Scottish “loch”.

mistakes.wrong: “gatto”, “mamma”, “difficile” (gato, mamá, difícil)
mistakes.right: gato, mamá, difícil: short consonants
mistakes.why: Italian has long consonants. Spanish doesn't, and many similar words are written with one consonant.

mistakes.wrong: pollo, calle with a long l, as in “bello”
mistakes.right: pollo, calle: y as in “yes”
mistakes.why: Italian ll is a long l. Spanish ll is another sound: in most of Spain, y.

mistakes.wrong: “kiko”, “koke” (chico, coche)
mistakes.right: chico, coche: ch as in “cena”
mistakes.why: Italian ch is k (chiesa). Spanish ch is the sound Italian writes c before e, i.

mistakes.wrong: casa, mesa with a buzzing s
mistakes.right: casa, mesa: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: In much of northern Italy, s between vowels buzzes. Spanish s doesn't.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with top teeth on the bottom lip
mistakes.right: vino, nuevo: only the lips
mistakes.why: Italian has a separate v sound. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: I have 30 years.
mistakes.why: Italian says ho 30 anni. English says: I'm 30, or I'm 30 years old.

mistakes.wrong: Is raining. Is late.
mistakes.right: It's raining. It's late.
mistakes.why: In Italian you can leave out the subject (Piove. È tardi.). An English sentence always needs one – often it.

languages.name: Arabic
strengths: Arabic has a definite article (al-), so the idea of “the” is not new to you.
Standard Arabic has the two th sounds (ث in think, ذ in this), so they are often easy for you.

mistakes.wrong: “bero”, “ban” (pero, pan)
mistakes.right: pero, pan: p without the voice
mistakes.why: Standard Arabic has no p, so it often becomes b. Put your fingers on your throat: for p nothing shakes until the vowel.

mistakes.wrong: “misa” for mesa, “luna” for lona
mistakes.right: mesa and misa, lona and luna: different words
mistakes.why: Arabic has three vowels (a, i, u), short or long. Spanish e and o lie between them, so they are easy to mix up.

mistakes.wrong: hola, hora with a clear ه
mistakes.right: “ola”, “ora”
mistakes.why: Arabic h is always said. Spanish h is silent.

mistakes.wrong: i live in london with my brother.
mistakes.right: I live in London with my brother.
mistakes.why: Arabic script has no capital and small letters. In English, I, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

mistakes.wrong: I have car. My brother engineer.
mistakes.right: I have a car. My brother is an engineer.
mistakes.why: Arabic has no word for a/an, and in the present it usually leaves out be. English needs both: a car, he is an engineer.

mistakes.wrong: This is the book that I bought it.
mistakes.right: This is the book that I bought.
mistakes.why: An Arabic relative clause repeats the thing with a pronoun (…alladhī ishtaraytuhu). In English the pronoun is not repeated.

languages.name: Russian
strengths: The usual Russian order is like the English one: Я люблю кофе – I love coffee.
Russian uses many international words that English has too: компьютер, музыка, телефон – computer, music, telephone.

mistakes.wrong: “tamate”, “karazón” (tomate, corazón)
mistakes.right: tomate, corazón: a clear o
mistakes.why: In Russian, o without stress sounds like a, and e like i. Spanish vowels keep their sound in every syllable.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with top teeth on the bottom lip (в)
mistakes.right: vino, nuevo: only the lips
mistakes.why: Russian в is a separate sound. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: zapato, plaza with a buzzing з
mistakes.right: zapato, plaza: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: Russian has no /θ/, and the letter z suggests з. In most of Spain z is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south s. Both are correct; the buzz isn't.

mistakes.wrong: I have question. It is good idea.
mistakes.right: I have a question. It's a good idea.
mistakes.why: Russian has no articles. In English, one countable thing needs a/an (or the).

mistakes.wrong: I live here since 2020.
mistakes.right: I've lived here since 2020.
mistakes.why: Russian uses the present for something that started in the past and is still true (Я живу здесь с 2020 года). English uses the present perfect.

mistakes.wrong: I student. He in London.
mistakes.right: I'm a student. He's in London.
mistakes.why: In Russian the present of be is left out (Я студент). English always needs am, is or are.

languages.name: Ukrainian
strengths: Ukrainian has a sound close to h (г), so English h is often easier for you than for Russian speakers.
The usual Ukrainian order is like the English one: subject – verb – object.

mistakes.wrong: “hato”, “amiho” (gato, amigo)
mistakes.right: gato, amigo: g as in ґ
mistakes.why: Ukrainian г is a breathy sound, close to h. Spanish g is closer to ґ, and softer between vowels.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with the sound of в
mistakes.right: vino, nuevo: only the lips
mistakes.why: Ukrainian в is a separate sound. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: zapato, plaza with a buzzing з
mistakes.right: zapato, plaza: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no /θ/, and the letter z suggests з. In most of Spain z is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south s. Both are correct; the buzz isn't.

mistakes.wrong: I'm looking for flat.
mistakes.right: I'm looking for a flat.
mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no articles. In English, a/an or the is easily missing then.

mistakes.wrong: I teacher.
mistakes.right: I'm a teacher.
mistakes.why: In Ukrainian the present of be is left out (Я вчителька). English needs am/is/are – and a before a job.

mistakes.wrong: You like tea?
mistakes.right: Do you like tea?
mistakes.why: Ukrainian makes a yes/no question with the voice only (Ти любиш чай?). English puts do/does at the start.

languages.name: Chinese
strengths: Like English, Chinese puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object: 我喝咖啡 – I drink coffee.
Chinese verbs have no person endings – and English has very few: only -s for he, she and it.

mistakes.wrong: “pelo” for pero, “hola” for hora
mistakes.right: pero and pelo, hora and hola: different words
mistakes.why: Mandarin has no tapped r, and r and l are easy to mix up. For l the tongue stays up; for r it taps once and goes.

mistakes.wrong: pan with a puff of air, bueno without any voice
mistakes.right: pan: no puff · bueno: voice on from the start
mistakes.why: Mandarin tells b and p apart by a puff of air. Spanish tells them apart by the voice: p has no puff, b has voice.

mistakes.wrong: “habla” for hablar, “ma” for mal
mistakes.right: hablar, mal: say the last sound
mistakes.why: Mandarin syllables end almost only in n, ng or a vowel. Spanish words often end in s, l, r or d, and the ending carries meaning.

mistakes.wrong: “te-ren”, “pu-laza” (tren, plaza)
mistakes.right: tren, plaza: no vowel between
mistakes.why: Mandarin syllables don't start with two consonants, so a vowel slips in. Spanish has many: pl-, tr-, gr-, fr-.

mistakes.wrong: He go to work. I have two brother.
mistakes.right: He goes to work. I have two brothers.
mistakes.why: In Chinese the verb never changes and nouns have no plural ending. In English: he/she/it + -s, and a plural -s on the noun.

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I go to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I went to the cinema.
mistakes.why: Chinese shows time with words like yesterday (昨天), not on the verb. English changes the verb too: go → went.

languages.name: Turkish
strengths: Turkish uses the Latin alphabet, so English letters are not new to you.
Turkish has ş and ç – the same sounds as sh and ch in ship and chair.

mistakes.wrong: I go school. I have question.
mistakes.right: I go to school. I have a question.
mistakes.why: Turkish has no articles and uses endings instead of prepositions (okul-a = to school). In English, to and a/an are words of their own.

mistakes.wrong: My sister – he is a doctor.
mistakes.right: My sister – she is a doctor.
mistakes.why: Turkish has one word for he, she and it: o. In English, choose he for a man, she for a woman and it for a thing.

mistakes.wrong: I every day coffee drink.
mistakes.right: I drink coffee every day.
mistakes.why: In Turkish the verb comes at the end. In English it comes right after the subject, and the object follows: I drink coffee.

mistakes.wrong: Where you live? You are coming?
mistakes.right: Where do you live? Are you coming?
mistakes.why: Turkish makes a question with the little word mi or a question word, and the order stays the same. English needs do/does, or puts the verb first: Are you coming?

languages.name: Persian (Farsi/Dari)
strengths: Persian and English are related (Indo-European). Some words are similar: pedar – father, mādar – mother, barādar – brother.
Persian has no grammatical gender – and English nouns don't have one either.

mistakes.wrong: tomorrow i have a doctor's appointment.
mistakes.right: Tomorrow I have a doctor's appointment.
mistakes.why: Persian script has no capital letters. In English, I and the first word of a sentence start with a capital.

mistakes.wrong: My brother – she lives in Leeds.
mistakes.right: My brother – he lives in Leeds.
mistakes.why: Persian has one word for he and she: u (او). In English, choose he for a man and she for a woman.

mistakes.wrong: I today English learn.
mistakes.right: I'm learning English today.
mistakes.why: In Persian the verb comes at the end of the sentence. In English it comes right after the subject.

languages.name: Polish
strengths: Polish has sounds very close to sh and ch in ship and chair (sz, cz).
Polish words often start with several consonants (strona, sprawa), so street and spring are easy for you.

mistakes.wrong: Where is station?
mistakes.right: Where is the station?
mistakes.why: Polish has no articles. In English the noun needs one.

mistakes.wrong: I have 30 years.
mistakes.why: Polish says mam 30 lat (I have 30 years). In English, age goes with be: I'm 30, or I'm 30 years old.

languages.name: Vietnamese
strengths: Vietnamese uses the Latin alphabet, so you can read English letters from day one.
A simple sentence has the same order as in English: Tôi uống cà phê – I drink coffee.

mistakes.wrong: I have car. Where is station?
mistakes.right: I have a car. Where is the station?
mistakes.why: Vietnamese has no articles. In English a countable noun almost always needs a/an or the.

mistakes.wrong: two book, three child
mistakes.right: two books, three children
mistakes.why: In Vietnamese, number words show the amount and the noun stays the same. In English the noun changes: -s, or an irregular plural (children).

mistakes.wrong: foot ball, birth day, bed room
mistakes.right: football, birthday, bedroom
mistakes.why: Vietnamese writes every syllable as a word of its own. Many English words have two or more syllables written together.

mistakes.wrong: Here has a café.
mistakes.right: There's a café here.
mistakes.why: Vietnamese có means both have and there is. English uses two expressions: I have … / There is …

languages.name: Tagalog
strengths: Tagalog uses the Latin alphabet, and many people in the Philippines learn English at school.
Many Tagalog words come from Spanish or English and are easy to recognise: telepono (telephone), kompyuter (computer).

mistakes.wrong: My sister works in Manchester. He is a nurse.
mistakes.right: My sister works in Manchester. She is a nurse.
mistakes.why: In Tagalog siya means he and she – the pronoun shows no gender. In English you choose: he for a man, she for a woman, it for a thing.

mistakes.wrong: She work in a hospital.
mistakes.right: She works in a hospital.
mistakes.why: Tagalog verbs don't change for the person. In the English present simple, he, she and it need -s: she works.

mistakes.wrong: Yesterday I work until 10 pm.
mistakes.right: Yesterday I worked until 10 pm.
mistakes.why: The Tagalog verb shows if something is finished or still going on (nagtrabaho, nagtatrabaho); when it happened often comes from the context. In English the past needs the past form: worked.

mistakes.wrong: Can you open the light?
mistakes.right: Can you turn on the light?
mistakes.why: Tagalog says buksan ang ilaw (open the light). In English you turn on / switch on a light, the TV or the air conditioning, and turn off / switch off.

mistakes.wrong: Here has a supermarket.
mistakes.right: There's a supermarket here.
mistakes.why: Tagalog may means have and there is: May kotse ako. – May supermarket dito. English uses two expressions: I have … / There is …

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Arabic or Persian as their first language write i and names with a small letter?
options: Their script has no capital letters
In Arabic everything is written in capitals
quiz.answer: Their script has no capital letters
quiz.explain: In English: I, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

quiz.prompt: How do you say your age correctly?
quiz.explain: I have 25 years comes from French, Italian, Spanish or Polish. English uses be: I'm 25 (years old).
She became a doctor. A false friend for German speakers: bekommen = get.

quiz.prompt: You moved here three years ago and you still live here. What is correct?
options: I've lived here for three years.
I live here since three years.
I'm living here since three years.
quiz.answer: I've lived here for three years.
quiz.explain: Still true now: present perfect, with for + a length of time.

quiz.prompt: Where does the verb usually go in an English sentence?
quiz.explain: I drink coffee every day. Tomorrow I'm going to London.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between bag and back?
options: The last sound: g has voice, k doesn't
quiz.answer: The last sound: g has voice, k doesn't
quiz.explain: In English the voice stays on at the end of bag, bed, dog – otherwise you say back, bet, dock.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between ship and sheep?
quiz.explain: ship: short /ɪ/. sheep: long /iː/. In English the length changes the meaning.

quiz.prompt: You feel cold. What do you say?
quiz.explain: I have cold comes from French (j'ai froid) or Spanish (tengo frío). Careful: I have a cold means you are ill.

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Vietnamese say “lie” instead of life?
options: Vietnamese syllables end in only a few consonants
The f in life is silent
quiz.answer: Vietnamese syllables end in only a few consonants
quiz.explain: In English you hear the last consonant: life, place, next.
